conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Rivera, a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—often shortened to the **EPDS**. It’s simply a set of 10 questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days, designed to pick up on signs of depression, anxiety, and to check on your overall emotional well-being during the postpartum period.

Everything you share today is confidential, and our conversation is a safe space—no judgment, just support. We’ll go through the questions one by one; you can take your time and answer in your own words. When you’re ready, we can start.

**Question 1.** In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve still been able to laugh sometimes—like when my partner makes a silly face at the baby—but it feels kind of forced. The funny side of things doesn’t come as easily as it used to; most of the time I’m just too tired or preoccupied.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I can still laugh, but it’s not the same. It feels like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment, and even when I do laugh, it fades fast.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes I do look forward to little stuff—like my mom coming over so I can take a shower without rushing—but the big things feel kind of flat. It’s more “okay, that’ll be nice” than real excitement.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like if the baby spits up a lot or won’t settle, I think maybe I ate something wrong or I’m not doing something right. I know it’s probably not my fault, but those thoughts still pop in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly my worry is about the baby—like if she’s breathing okay or if I’m missing some sign that something’s wrong. It’s not totally out of nowhere, but it does feel bigger than it probably should. Sometimes I’ll be holding her, everything’s fine, and my heart’s still racing.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times, yeah—like last night when I was feeding her in the dark, my chest got tight and I felt this sudden wave of “something bad is about to happen.” I knew it didn’t make sense, but I couldn’t shake it for a few minutes.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… some days it feels like the minute I finish one thing, the baby needs something else, and the dishes and laundry just keep piling up. I’ll be rocking her with one foot while scrolling my phone, thinking, “I can’t keep up,” and it makes me want to cry, even though I hardly ever do.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I’m tired all the time, but when I finally lie down, my brain won’t settle—kept running through “did I sterilize the bottles?” or “is she gaining enough weight?” I wouldn’t call it being unhappy, more like I can’t shut the worries off.
I have felt sad or miserable
I do feel sad some moments—like when I’m sitting alone feeding her at 3 a.m. and it feels like the rest of the world is asleep. It’s not every day, but those waves hit me a few times this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t cried much—maybe once or twice all week. I felt teary a couple of other times, but I managed to hold it in. Mostly I just feel heavy, like a weight on my chest, rather than full-on sobbing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like myself again and be a good mom.

You've shared that new motherhood has felt heavy lately-laughing takes effort, excitement is muted, and waves of worry or sadness catch you off-guard, especially during quiet night feeds. You're working hard to care for your baby while feeling overwhelmed by chores and self-doubt, yet you remain committed to being a "good mom" and have not had thoughts of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 16, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to laugh and enjoy moments, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment for "big things" and only mild anticipation for small events, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>She acknowledges self-blame 'some of the time,' recognizing it's likely unwarranted.</sym>, <sym>Acknowledges worry about baby is common but describes physical anxiety symptoms and racing heart, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty keeping up with daily tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurrent waves of sadness several times this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 16 places you well above the 14-point cutoff indicating probable major depressive disorder with peripartum onset. Core criteria are met: diminished interest/pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), self-reproach, anxiety, sadness, and functional difficulty keeping up with daily tasks. These symptoms have persisted most days over the past week, cause distress, and are a change from your usual self, aligning with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Absence of self-harm thoughts is noted and is reassuring for safety planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, other psychotherapy, or medication compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share these results and your support needs with a trusted partner or family member so they can help with baby care and household tasks
4. Practice 15-20 min daily of guided relaxation or deep breathing; consider apps designed for postpartum anxiety
5. Aim for one 3-4 hr stretch of uninterrupted sleep per 24 hrs-accept help for night bottles or pump-and-sleep arrangements
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and intervention response
7. Maintain pediatric appointments; inform your baby's provider so they can support feeding and bonding goals
8. If feelings worsen or you ever consider self-harm, call 988 (US) or your local emergency number immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Screening note – EPDS-style interview, 2–3 wk postpartum

Symptoms endorsed  
– Markedly diminished enjoyment/pleasure (laughing “not the same,” anticipatory anhedonia)  
– Excessive guilt/blame re infant care  
– Persistent, intrusive worry about infant safety; episodic panic sensations (chest tightness, dread)  
– Frequent sense of being overwhelmed; tearfulness when alone  
– Subjective sadness, especially during night feeds; “heavy” chest sensation  
– Initial insomnia driven by racing, infant-focused ruminations  

Pattern  
Mood, pleasure, and coping consistently lowered; anxiety symptoms prominent and intrusive; no frank depressive tearfulness, yet clear emotional heaviness and intermittent panic.  
Functional theme: “can’t keep up” with basic tasks, intrusive vigilance about infant.

Screening significance  
Meets threshold concern for postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features; rule-out postpartum anxiety disorder.  
No self-harm ideation reported → current safety risk absent.

Summary  
Patient demonstrates multiple affective and anxiety symptoms typical of perinatal mood disturbance; further assessment (formal EPDS scoring, clinical interview, differential for GAD/panic) warranted to clarify severity and inform next-level care.
